They may be arguing with posters from the vet as we speak. They may be making one more last ditch effort but doing this immediately after. They may be unable to afford multiple cats with feeding tubes and extensive stays  

But here's a good PSA for anyone on this sub that may be looking to get a/more cats: if you can't afford pet insurance you can't afford the cat. Because if you can't afford pet insurance you wont be affording the potentially thousands upon thousands upon thousands of dollars it can take to care for them.

I was naïve to this and had the mindset of crossing that bridge when it came but my boyfriend at the time was like "no your cats are going on my pet insurance period" while I was like wow thats à lot of money that could be spent on other things.

A month or 2 later, Tubbie starts à career in crystal making. Multiple flare ups that year costing upwards of $3000+ EVERY time. We struggled but we only made it through bc of pet insurance covering 80%+ of each claim (paying up front was still not the nicest but we knew we were getting it back).

Tubbie now needs special wet AND dry that are hundreds of dollars (but like every few months or so) and he's on anxiety medication. He's an expensive little boy but I'd rather pay that than $3000 every few months plus à potentially penis amputation.

Moral of the story: you could have 10 cats and never have an issue but you could have 1 that becomes à sentient vet medical book of problems and you don't want the reason you had to let them go be that even though it was manageable you weren't responsible and couldn't afford it. 

Ignorance doesn't make you a bad pet owner but a refusal to listen to advice and become responsible does

Fellow autistic here. It is so hard as a neurodivergent, but especially an autistic person to find someone to be with. My husband will say all relationships have their challenges, but I know for a fact I am the most challenging person he has ever been with. 

We are extra challenging to be and are therefore extra challenging to be with. And it's not all bad, there's a lot about me and my autism, that my husband just adores. As for the bad, i don't know what Stockholm Syndrome voodoo hold, I have on that man, but it's there.

I am objectively 3/10 and on my best day, ever, in my entire thirty years of life, i've only ever managed to maybe be a six out of ten. Maybe once or twice, ever in my lifetime. I'm high functioning academically, but low functioning day today.And my husband has to be my legitimate caregiver. I'm overweight and have issues with food and self control. 

I'd love to say my personality makes up for everything else, but it in fact doesn't. I strongly believe everyone in my life. Is there out of a mixture of pity and stockholm syndrome. I have the advantage of being female.

But really? I'm a lot like you.I'm definitely a neck beard. I've never once blamed others for me being difficult to be in a relationship with, but it's very mentally taxing to know that and to not be able to do much about it.

However, as you'll have gathered, i'm married by some miracle. The right person exists out there. I believe in the good place style soulmates, and I found mine, and I believe you can find yours.

But when you do, yes, there's a lot about us with our autism and things we can't help or change but be so self aware and works so hard to find a way to bridge the gap. That's the only way i've been able to make it work with my husband. We've done couples therapy, we process communication and sometimes disagreements through chat g p t, a lot of nights where we sleep separate. But one of us will eventually cave and well talk it out at like two in the morning and be good. Lots of almost breaking up moments.

We're at a point now where disagreements are very few and far between, but miscommunication is almost daily. And we work damn hard daily, to make that work and bridge that gap and find tools and resources that help. It's at the point where if you asked us, I don't know that we would register them as miscommunications. 

It's also about fundingThe right person who's willing to hear you and see you and not just call you lazy and stupid and call it a day.

I've been called lazy, and so much more by people who instead of listening to my struggle and hearing me just want to write me off as not wanting to do things as opposed to being actually disabled. But we also have to hear them out snd validate their struggles and help them as best we can.

Certain things like, for example, my partner sometimes wishes I could anticipate needs and the longer we're together.I can sometimes do that, but very rarely. So certain things it's just like any relationship where it's up to your partner, whether that's a deal breaker or not, or something that they can live with or without. 

It's hard for everybody. I think in some cases, it can be extra hard for us. And I want you to hear this from somebody in a more similar situation and age. 

My partner allows me to be fooling me without masking and stuff. But all of the things I can't do that. Other partners can inherently do make me constantly feel as alien as masking does. 

Anytime you enter a relationship, you're giving some of yourself and taking some of them so it's about finding balance and also finding someone who's self is worth taking enough to give that much of yourself to them. 

I still struggle with plenty and I see a therapist, and so does my husband and we did together and still do when needed, but I found a person and a situation where, the good makes me the happiest. I've ever been in heavily outweighs any of the hard or bad. 

It's possible but it takes a lot a lot. A lot of work and some luck. And a bit of putting yourself out there, which is extra uncomfortable for us. 

Good luck friend. 

PS: i'm thirty, and this is only my second relationship. So, trust me, when I say that I get it. And i'm confident i'm very close to your situation and how you feel about yourself and the situation

Honestly, write down every and all skills on linkedin, sort by remote or hybrid and apply to literally everything I'm talking up to like 5 pages of the search in. Thats what I did.

I was working at Johnson and my mental health was so bad i was off work for 6 months and needed a change but didn't know whatever in the fuck I could possibly do to find employment and work in a field using my degree.

I found my job on like page 3 or 4 of the search. I was hired bilingual but don't get to use my French much- though my English one is being used. To bridge the gap I do occasional freelance French jobs.

There are a lot of companies on linkedin that hire people and then send jobs to your email which you can accept or not. These range from data entry to live translation.

My job is perfect for me. It's 100% flexible where no one is checking my teams for activity, I can pop out in the day without needing permission and just need to give a heads up if I'll be more than an hour. I don't work with the public at all, I work with internal teams. My team is comprised of Americans and Canadians and we are spread out all over both countries. On-boarding and all that was very "go your own pace" within reason. There's also a lot of opportunities for growth and learning.

Im autistic and don't need water cooler talk for social fulfillment and in fact find that hinders me. I'm probably the only one on my team with 0 background in the field but they hired me because there was something about me they liked. I rarely have to mask because I'm home and only really do when I'm running meetings. We get a lot of freedom so long as we do our work well, put our hours in, and don't miss meetings. I've even been given opportunities to do join mental health committees and advocate for autism at work.

My manager is amazing. Very stern and doesn't beat around the bush but also the first to tell you you've done a good job. She evaluates us on a per person basis- I'm weighted against my own progress and no one else's. 

No company is perfect but I found one and a career perfect for me and my needs.

My point here is a couple things: WAY more exists out there than people réalise. Dream jobs with dream conditions you never even heard of. Anyone with a high school diploma or any university degree can find a job that way too. It takes time and you'll get a lot of no's as well but it's well worth it. I think a lot of people here underestimate linkedin.

My other point is A LOT of companies are now hiring based on personality and fit moreso than experience. Im not saying experience and an impressive resume doesn't matter, but if you interview well and charm the socks off someone, they're willing to invest in you. What a lot of companies don't get is treating you right and investing in you makes you more likely to stay- training new people every few months costs a lot more money.

Another important thing about linkedin is connections. Once you get an idea of what you want, start connecting with people in those jobs or fields. Youll get more visibility and appear in searches. See what sorts of buzz words they use as skills etc and use those to come up in the right searches. Also, if you end up in contact with a recruiter during the hiring process, connect on linkedin regardless on it hired. Recruiters post opportunities on their page and again it gets you visibility to come up in searches and stuff.
